title: Writing a reviewable pull request
summary: How to shape a change so a maintainer can review it fast: one logical change per PR, commits that each build, a title and description that explain why, correct issue links, a self-review pass, and drafts.
outcomes: Explain why reviewers ask for large PRs to be split and judge when a PR is too large or too small
Split a tangled change into a stack of focused PRs whose commits each build and stay bisectable
Write a title and description that state the problem, approach, where to look and what was left out
Predict when a closing keyword like Closes #123 links and closes an issue, and when GitHub ignores it
Run a self-review pass and use draft PRs to signal readiness honestly

lessons.title: Why a reviewer sends a big pull request back

blocks.md:
You already know the mechanics: fork, branch, commit, push, open a pull request (PR), and you know to read CONTRIBUTING before you start. This course is about the part those steps leave open: shaping the change itself so that a busy maintainer can review it quickly and confidently.

A **reviewable** PR is one a reviewer can understand, verify and approve without reconstructing your thinking. Most PRs that stall are not wrong. They are hard to review.

Here is the running example for the whole course. You find a bug in a project's LRU cache (a cache that evicts the least recently used entry when full): expired entries still count toward the size limit, so the cache evicts live entries too early. While fixing it you also rename the module from `lru.py` to `cache/lru.py` and speed up the lookup path. You open one PR with all of it: about 640 changed lines.

blocks.prompt: The maintainer is friendly and the fix is correct. What is the most likely first response to the 640-line PR?
blocks.reveal: Most likely: **please split this up**. Google's engineering practices guide says reviewers "have discretion to reject your change outright for the sole reason of it being too large", and usually ask for "a series of smaller changes" instead. The fix you care about is 38 of the 640 lines, buried among a rename and an optimization the reviewer has to check separately.

blocks.md: Why does size matter so much? The reviewer, unlike you, starts with no context. Google's guide lists what small changes buy: they are reviewed more quickly (it is easier to find five minutes several times than a 30-minute block), reviewed more thoroughly, less likely to introduce bugs, less wasted work if rejected, easier to merge and simpler to roll back.

blocks.title: One reviewer's afternoon: one big PR vs three small ones

scenes.caption: The reviewer has other work. Their free gaps are 10, 10, 10 and 35 minutes long. A PR is only reviewed when it fits in a gap.
The 640-line PR needs an uninterrupted 30 minutes. The first gap that long starts at minute 150, so first feedback arrives at minute 180.
Split into three focused PRs of about 5 minutes each, the first is reviewed by minute 25 and all three by minute 100, using gaps the big PR could not use.
Simplified model: the 5 and 30 minute durations are the examples from Google's guide, not measurements. Real reviews also depend on familiarity and risk.

blocks.md: Real data agrees. In a study of code review at Google (Sadowski et al., ICSE SEIP 2018), the median change modified **24 lines**, over 35% of changes touched a single file, and the median wait for first feedback was under an hour for small changes but about 5 hours for very large ones. The same paper notes that median change sizes in open source projects are similarly small.

blocks.title: Median lines modified per change (Sadowski et al. 2018)

scenes.caption: Median change size at Google is 24 lines; the paper compares it with 44 at AMD and 263 at Lucent, figures it cites from Rigby and Bird.

blocks.md: So what counts as small? Google's guide gives a rule of thumb, not a law: about **100 lines** is usually reasonable and **1000 lines** is usually too large. File count matters too: a 200-line change in one file might be fine, but spread across 50 files it usually is not. Deleting a whole file counts as roughly one line, and a large change produced by a trusted automated refactoring tool can be bigger.
The right size for a PR is **one self-contained change**: it does one thing, includes its tests, and leaves the system working. Line counts are a symptom; focus is the goal.
Misconception: "small" means "tiny". Google's guide also says a change can be too small to understand: if you add a new API, include a use of it in the same change so reviewers can judge it.

blocks.question: A contributor's PR adds a new public function `parse_duration()` but no caller, promising "the caller comes in the next PR". What is the strongest review concern?
options: The PR is too large and should be split further
The PR is too small to judge: without a use, reviewers cannot tell if the API is right
New functions always need a separate design document first
It should be a draft because it has no tests
blocks.explain: Google's small CL guide says a change should not be so small that its implications are hard to understand; adding an API with a usage lets reviewers see how it will be used and avoids checking in unused APIs.

blocks.question: Which PR is most likely to be flagged as too large, according to Google's guidance?
options: A 200-line bug fix in one file
A change that only deletes three obsolete files (900 removed lines)
A 200-line change spread across 50 files
A 60-line change with 40 lines of tests
blocks.explain: Size includes spread. The guide says a 200-line change in one file might be okay, but across 50 files it would usually be too large. Deleting whole files counts as roughly one line each, and tests belong in the change.

lessons.title: One logical change per PR, and every commit builds

blocks.md: The Linux kernel's patch guide states the rule most projects share: **separate each logical change into a separate patch**. Its examples: a bug fix and a performance improvement to the same driver go in separate patches; an API change and a new driver that uses it go in two patches. The flip side matters too: if you make a single change to many files, group it in one patch.

Apply that to the cache PR. It contains three logical changes with very different review needs:

- **Rename** `lru.py` to `cache/lru.py` (about 410 lines, mechanical, no behavior change).
- **Fix** expired entries counting toward the size limit, plus a regression test (38 lines).
- **Speedup** of the lookup path (192 lines), which needs benchmark numbers.

A reviewer checks a rename by confirming nothing else changed, a fix by reading the test, and a speedup by looking at measurements. Mixed together, they must do all three at once on every hunk.

blocks.title: Splitting the cache PR into a stack

nodes.label:
PR 1: move lru.py
no behavior change

scenes.caption: The tangled PR: one reviewer must check a rename, a bug fix and an optimization in the same 640-line diff.
Pull the move into its own PR first. The kernel guide says moved code should not be modified in the patch that moves it, so the reviewer only confirms an exact move.
Stack the fix on top: write the next PR on the first one's branch while it is in review (Google calls this stacking). PR 2 holds only the 38-line fix and its test.
The speedup goes last, with numbers. Each PR is justifiable on its own and can be reviewed by the right person; the fix can merge even if the speedup is debated.

blocks.md: Google's guide lists ways to split: stacking (start the next change on top of the one in review), by files that need different reviewers, horizontally by layer (for example API stub then implementation), vertically by feature, and separating refactorings from behavior changes. Small cleanups like renaming a local variable can stay in a fix.

Splitting creates a new obligation. The kernel guide says to ensure the tree **builds and runs properly after each patch** in a series, because developers using `git bisect` may land on any commit. Bisect does a binary search between a known good commit and a known bad one, so it tests roughly $\log_2 N$ commits for $N$ candidates. The git manual's example: 675 revisions left takes "roughly 10 steps" ($\log_2 675 \approx 9.4$).

blocks.title: git bisect over an 8-commit series (real run)

scenes.caption: A bug arrived somewhere in c1 to c8; c0 (before c1) is good and c8 is bad. Run with git bisect run and a test script that fails from c6 on.
Git checks out c4 first ("3 revisions left, roughly 2 steps"). The test passes, so c1 to c4 are cleared.
Next it tests c6: it fails. The culprit is c5 or c6.
c5 passes, so git reports c6 as the first bad commit after 3 tests, matching log2(8) = 3. Because c6 is one focused change, its diff explains the bug.
Same series, but c5 is a half-done refactor that does not build, so the script skips it. Git stops with "the first bad commit could be any of" c5 and c6.

blocks.md: That last scene is what a broken intermediate commit costs. The git-bisect manual warns that if you skip a commit adjacent to the one you are looking for, Git cannot tell which was the first bad one. A series where every commit builds and passes tests keeps the history bisectable.

If the project squash-merges PRs, your intermediate commits disappear from the main branch anyway, and the PR as a whole becomes one commit. That makes **one logical change per PR** even more important: the squash cannot separate a fix from a speedup after the fact.
Each PR (and each commit in a series) should be justifiable on its own and leave the project building and passing tests. If one depends on another, say so in the description.

blocks.question: Your PR moves `parser.c` into `lib/` and, while there, fixes an off-by-one in the moved function. What does the kernel guide recommend?
options: Keep both in one patch so the history shows the fix where the code now lives
Fix the bug first, then move the code in a second patch, or move first and fix second, but never modify code in the patch that moves it
Move the code and reformat it in the same patch, but put the fix separately
Leave the move out entirely; moves are never accepted
blocks.explain: The guide says not to modify moved code at all in the patch that moves it. That keeps the move verifiable as a pure move, and the fix shows up as a small, readable diff that history tools can track.

blocks.question: A 5-commit series has commit 3 that does not compile (it was fixed in commit 4). Why might a maintainer ask you to fix this before merging with a merge commit?
options: Because git bisect may land on commit 3 and be unable to test it, hiding which commit introduced a later bug
Because CI only tests the first commit
Because GitHub refuses to merge a PR with a broken commit
Because commit 3 doubles the review time
blocks.explain: A merge commit keeps every commit on the main branch. Bisect can check out any of them; an untestable commit must be skipped, and if it is next to the culprit, git cannot say which one is first bad.

lessons.title: A title and description that explain why

blocks.md: The diff shows **what** changed. Only you can say **why**. Google's guide calls the description "a public record of change" that must say what is being changed and why, including decisions not reflected in the code. GitHub's own guidance asks for the problem, the approach, and where reviewers should pay special attention.

The title is the most-read line you will write. Git's manual suggests starting a commit message with a short summary line (no more than 50 characters as a soft limit), then a blank line, then the body; Git uses that first line as the title everywhere, for example as the email subject in `git format-patch`. The kernel caps its summary phrase at 70 to 75 characters. Many projects prefix the area: Git's own convention is `area: summary`, such as `doc: clarify ...`.

blocks.prompt: Rank these titles for a reviewer scanning 30 PRs: (a) `Fix bug` (7 characters), (b) `cache: evict expired entries before size check` (46 characters), (c) `Fix bug where the LRU cache would sometimes keep expired entries around even after they should have been evicted` (112 characters).
blocks.reveal: **(b) is best.** (a) is on Google's list of bad descriptions: what bug, and what did you do? (c) has the facts but is over twice Git's 50-character guideline, so it crowds one-line views like `git log --oneline` and email subjects, where the kernel guide notes the summary is often all people see. (b) names the area, says what the change does in the imperative mood, and fits in 46 characters.

blocks.title: Reading the cache fix's PR description
blocks.code:
cache: evict expired entries before size check

LRUCache.put() checks len(self._data) >= max_size before
it removes expired entries. Expired entries therefore count
toward the limit, and a full cache evicts live entries that
callers still use. With max_size=2, live key A (least
recently used) and expired key B, put(C) evicts A, not B.

Purge expired entries first, then apply the size check.

Where to look: put() in cache/lru.py. The test in
tests/test_lru.py reproduces the eviction and fails on main.

Not changed: get() still expires lazily; a background sweeper
was considered and left for a separate discussion.

Depends on #241 (move lru.py into cache/).
Closes #123

scenes.caption: Title: area prefix, imperative mood ("evict", not "evicted" or "this PR evicts"), 46 characters. It must make sense alone in a list.
The problem first, in the present tense, with a concrete trigger. The kernel guide says to convince the reviewer there is a problem worth reading past the first paragraph.
The approach in one plain sentence, so the reviewer can check the code does what you intended.
Where to look: point the reviewer at the one function that matters and at the test that fails without the fix.
What you chose not to do and why. Git's SubmittingPatches asks for alternatives considered but discarded, which saves a review round.
Dependencies and links. The closing keyword links issue #123 and closes it on merge, if this PR targets the default branch.

blocks.md:
A few rules from the kernel and Git guides that apply to any project:

- **Quantify optimizations.** If you claim a speedup or memory saving, include the numbers and the non-obvious costs.
- **Be self-contained.** Summarize the discussion rather than only linking to it; links rot and later readers may lack access. When you push a new version, keep the full description current instead of writing "v2".
- **Imperative mood.** "Make xyzzy do frotz", not "This patch makes xyzzy do frotz".

Now the issue link. GitHub recognizes nine closing keywords: close, closes, closed, fix, fixes, fixed, resolve, resolves, resolved, followed by `#number` (or `owner/repo#number` for another repository). They work in the PR description or in a commit message, are case-insensitive and may take a colon (`Closes: #10`). Each issue needs its own keyword.

blocks.title: When Closes #123 actually closes the issue

scenes.caption: PR 2 is stacked on PR 1, so it targets PR 1's branch, not main. You put Closes #123 in its description.
GitHub ignores the keyword: closing keywords are interpreted only when the PR targets the default branch. No link is created.
PR 1 merges and you retarget PR 2 to main. Now the keyword is read and the issue shows the linked PR.
When PR 2 is merged into main, GitHub closes the issue automatically.

blocks.md: Do not write `Closes #123` on a PR that only partly addresses the issue: merging it will close the issue for everyone. Write "Part of #123" or "Refs #123" (neither is a closing keyword).

Title: what the change does, short enough for one-line views. Body: the problem and its impact, the approach, where to look, what you left out, and links. The description outlives the review: Google notes it may be read by hundreds of people over the years.

blocks.question: A project uses squash merging, and GitHub's default squash message can include the PR title and description. You titled the PR `wip` and left the body empty. What is the lasting cost?
options: The main branch can get a commit titled `wip` with no explanation, which future readers of git log and git blame will see
None: squash merging discards the PR title
GitHub blocks squash merges of PRs with short titles
Only the review is slowed; history is unaffected
blocks.explain: GitHub's docs say the default squash commit message can include the PR title and description. A maintainer can edit it, but a vague title often ends up as the permanent commit summary.

blocks.question: Which description best follows the kernel and Google guidance for a performance PR?
options: "Optimize lookup. Should be faster."
"v2 of the patch, see previous thread for details."
"Cache each key's hash so lookup skips rehashing. Before and after timings from bench_lookup are below; the cost is one extra word of memory per entry."
"This PR makes lookup faster and also renames lru.py."
blocks.explain: The kernel guide asks you to quantify optimizations and describe non-obvious costs, and to keep each version self-contained instead of pointing at earlier threads. Option 4 also mixes two logical changes.

lessons.title: Self-review the diff, then use drafts to signal readiness

blocks.md: Before asking anyone else, review your own PR. GitHub's guidance says a self-review can include reading the diff, checking for accidental changes, and making sure relevant builds or tests have run, and that it shows reviewers the PR is ready for their attention. Every stray debug print you catch is one review comment and one round trip you save.

blocks.title: A self-review pass before asking for review

nodes.label:
read Files changed
as a stranger

scenes.caption: git add -p shows each hunk and asks whether to stage it, so you review every change before it enters a commit and can leave unrelated edits out.
git diff --check flags whitespace errors. Git's own SubmittingPatches says the project is picky about whitespace and asks you to run it before committing.
Run the tests and the project's linters locally. The kernel guide warns a patch with basic style violations may be rejected without being read.
Read the Files changed tab as if you had never seen the code. Here you spot a leftover print() and an unrelated formatting change.
Go back, unstage the stray edits, amend, and run the pass again. This loop costs minutes; the same issues found by a reviewer cost a round trip each.

Clean pass. Re-read the description so it still matches the change after these edits, then ask for review. Google advises the same check again before the change lands, since changes can shift during review.

blocks.code:
git fetch upstream
git rebase upstream/main          # current base, no stale conflicts
git add -p                         # stage only what belongs
git diff --cached --check          # whitespace errors in staged changes
git commit -s                      # sign off if the project requires DCO
git log --oneline upstream/main..  # one focused commit per logical step?
git diff --stat upstream/main...   # files and lines a reviewer will see
blocks.caption: A pre-review routine using the workflow from the prerequisite course. The last two commands show the PR as a reviewer will see it.

blocks.md: Next, signal readiness honestly. GitHub lets you open a **draft pull request**. Drafts cannot be merged, and code owners (the people or teams listed for paths in a CODEOWNERS file) are not automatically requested to review them. Drafts are for sharing work in progress, asking an early design question, or watching CI, without formally requesting review.

blocks.title: Draft to ready: who gets asked, and when

scenes.caption: You open the fix as a draft to check the approach. GitHub will not let anyone merge it.
Code owners of cache/ are not auto-requested for drafts, so you are not spending their attention yet.
You self-review, push the cleanup, and finish the description.
Marking the PR ready for review requests reviews from the code owners. This is the moment you are asking for their time.
The owner asks for a larger change. GitHub's docs suggest converting back to draft to show more work is needed; it cannot be merged until marked ready again.

blocks.md: Use the project's PR template if it has one: GitHub fills it in from `pull_request_template.md` (in the root, `docs/` or `.github/`). GitHub suggests templates ask for a reference to the related issue, a description of the proposed changes, and mentions of who is responsible for reviewing.

Misconception: "I will clean it up after review starts." Reviewers read what is there. Opening a non-draft PR with failing tests, debug code or an empty description tells them it is ready when it is not, and spends their first pass on things you could have caught.
Self-review first, then mark ready. A reviewable PR is focused, explained, clean, and honestly labeled as draft or ready.

blocks.question: You want early feedback on whether your approach to a cache fix is acceptable, but tests are still failing. What is the best move?
options: Open a normal PR and ask code owners to ignore the failures
Wait until the change is finished before showing anyone
Open a normal PR with "WIP" in the title so it cannot be merged
Open a draft PR, state the open question in the description, and mark it ready once tests pass
blocks.explain: A draft cannot be merged and does not auto-request code owners, so it is the right tool for early feedback. A WIP title is only a convention: GitHub does not block merging on it.

blocks.question: During self-review you find that your editor reformatted 300 lines in a file you only touched for a 4-line fix. What should you do?
options: Leave it; formatting changes are harmless
Mention it in the description so reviewers can skip it
Unstage the reformatting (for example with git add -p) so the PR contains only the fix; send formatting separately if the project wants it
Squash it into the fix commit so the history is shorter
blocks.explain: Accidental changes are exactly what self-review is for. They bury the real change and cause merge conflicts for others. Formatting-only changes, if wanted, are their own logical change.
